newsitem.title: UK: Business reassured as UK drops merger change plans.
newsitem.headline: Business reassured as UK drops merger change plans.

text.p: Britain's business community on Wednesday welcomed news that Margaret Beckett, the new trade and industry minister, had dropped plans to make companies prove that any planned takeovers would be in the public interest.

"We're very reassured that she's leaving policy based on competitiveness rather than anything else -- which is how markets should work," noted a spokeswoman for The British Chambers of Commerce, the largest business representative body in Britian.

Speculation has been rife that the new Labour government, which swept to power in a landslide election victory in May, might change the burden of proof for mergers which have been referred to competition authorities.
Business groups, which said the decision to take over or merge had to be taken by the market without state intervention, noted that talk of such "meddling" had made them to "go slightly pale".

"The worry was that you'd start talking about national interest and forget about economic efficiency -- but that seems as if that has evaporated," said a spokeswoman for the Institute of Directors (IoD) employers group.
"But clearly whatever the speculation was at the beginning of May, she (Beckett) has retracted and I think that is right... We're a great believer in leaving things to the market," she added.

Despite research showing that mergers are not necessarily economically efficient, Beckett told industrialists in a keynote speech that competition grounds should be the primary consideration in takeovers under the new government.

She also told the business community that Labour was abandoning plans to merge the two competition regulatory bodies -- the Office of Fair Trading (OFT) and the Monopolies and Mergers Commission (MMC).

The Institute of Directors said it "seemed sensible" to keep the two bodies apart, adding that it would like to see less interference from the Department of Trade and Industry before cases were referred to the MMC.
Currently, the OFT can only recommend that the Department of Trade and Industry refers certain cases for a lengthy MMC investigation.

"I think there's too much screening at an initial stage," the IOD spokeswoman said. But she added that the elected government should take the final decision about whether to allow or ban a merger after an MMC referral.

The British Chambers of Commerce (BCC) also welcomed Beckett's pledge to work in partnership with business and trade unions, but warned that there must be no return to the "worst traditions of 1970s corporatism" when bureaucracy was overblown and inefficient.

Beckett said she wanted to set up an advisory group on competitiveness to offer practical and informed advice from business people across the range of sectors and types and size of firms -- and create a number of working groups to advise on specific aspects of competitiveness.
"We welcome any attempt to improve common understanding of the requirements for business competitiveness," BCC deputy director-general Ian Peters said.

"But any new group must have a precise purpose, a real problem to solve. We are not prepared to negotiate through national structures with employee representatives, the best place for negotiations is in the workplace," he added.
